items.title: Percentage — conversions, change & the comparison trap
items.body:
## Core relations

- **x% = x/100**; percentage *of* a quantity = quantity x %/100; whole = part x 100/%.
- **Increase / decrease%** = (change / original value) x 100 — always on the *original*.

## Fraction <-> percentage table (memorise)

| Fraction | % | Fraction | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/2 | 50% | 1/8 | 12.5% |
| 1/3 | 33.33% | 3/8 | 37.5% |
| 1/4 | 25% | 5/8 | 62.5% |
| 1/5 | 20% | 1/6 | 16.66% |
| 1/16 | 6.25% | 1/20 | 5% |

## Successive change (net single %)

- Two changes a% then b%: **net = a + b + ab/100** (use + for rise, - for fall).
- Equal +x% then -x% => net **-x^2/100 %** (never zero): +20% then -20% = -4%.

## The comparison / base-change trap

- 'A is x% more than B' => **B is x/(100+x) x 100 % less than A** (25% more => 20% less).
- Price up x% => **cut consumption by x/(100+x) x 100 %** to hold expenditure (25% up => 20% cut).

**Worked example:** A number is increased by 25% then decreased by 20%. Net = 25 - 20 + (25)(-20)/100 = 5 - 5 = **0%** — the number is unchanged.
keyPoints: x% = x/100; part = whole x %/100; whole = part x 100/%.
Increase/decrease% is always computed on the ORIGINAL value.
Successive change a% then b% = a + b + ab/100 (with signs).
Equal +x% then -x% gives a net -x^2/100 %, never zero.
A is x% more than B => B is x/(100+x)x100 % less than A.
Price up x% => reduce consumption by x/(100+x)x100 % to keep expenditure constant.
items.source: local APPSC Group-1 Quantitative Reasoning PDFs — Basic Percentage.txt, Successive Percentage Change.txt, Comparison of Percentage.txt

items.title: Simple Interest — formula, rearrangements & multiples
items.body:
## Formula

- **SI = P x R x T / 100**;  Amount **A = P + SI = P(1 + RT/100)**.
- Interest accrues on the **original principal only** — the base never grows.

## Rearranged forms

| Find | Formula |
|---|---|
| Principal P | 100 x SI / (R x T) |
| Rate R | 100 x SI / (P x T) |
| Time T | 100 x SI / (P x R) |

## Becoming a multiple of itself

- A sum **doubles** when total SI = P, i.e. **R x T = 100** (doubles in 8 yrs => R = 12.5%).
- To become **n times**: **R x T = (n - 1) x 100** (triples => RT = 200).

**Worked example:** A sum yields Rs 400 SI in 4 years at 5%. P = 100 x 400/(5 x 4) = 40000/20 = **Rs 2,000**.

**Common trap:** confusing the *time* (years) with the *rate* (%) in doubling problems.
keyPoints: SI = PRT/100; Amount = P(1 + RT/100); interest is on the original principal only.
P = 100xSI/(RxT); R = 100xSI/(PxT); T = 100xSI/(PxR).
A sum doubles under SI when R x T = 100.
To become n times under SI: R x T = (n - 1) x 100.
Doubling in 8 years under SI needs R = 12.5%.
items.source: local APPSC Group-1 Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Simple Interest.txt

items.title: Compound Interest — compounding, CI-SI gap & growth/decay
items.body:
## Formula

- **A = P(1 + R/100)^n**;  **CI = A - P = P[(1 + R/100)^n - 1]**.
- Interest is added to the principal each period, so the base grows.

## Compounding frequency

| Frequency | Rate per period | No. of periods |
|---|---|---|
| Annual | R | n |
| Half-yearly | R/2 | 2n |
| Quarterly | R/4 | 4n |

## CI - SI difference (same P, R, T)

- **2 years: CI - SI = P(R/100)^2.**
- **3 years: CI - SI = P(R/100)^2 x (3 + R/100).**

## Growth & decay (same machinery)

- Population / appreciation: **P(1 + R/100)^n**;  depreciation / decay: **P(1 - R/100)^n**.

**Worked example:** CI on Rs 10,000 at 10% p.a., compounded half-yearly for 1 year: rate 5%, periods 2 => 10000 x (1.05)^2 = 11,025 => CI = **Rs 1,025** (vs Rs 1,000 annual SI).

**Common trap:** for half-yearly, halve the rate AND double the periods — doing only one is the usual error.
keyPoints: Half-yearly => rate R/2 for 2n periods; quarterly => R/4 for 4n periods.
Compound growth = P(1+R/100)^n; depreciation/decay = P(1-R/100)^n.
More frequent compounding gives a higher effective yield.
items.mnemonic: Half-yearly = HALF the rate, DOUBLE the periods.
items.source: local APPSC Group-1 Quantitative Reasoning PDFs — Compound Interest.txt, Depreciation.txt

items.title: Profit, Loss, Discount & the CP=100 shortcut
items.body:
## Core formulae (percentages on Cost Price)

- **Profit% = (SP - CP)/CP x 100**;  **Loss% = (CP - SP)/CP x 100**.
- **SP = CP(1 + profit%/100)** or CP(1 - loss%/100).
- Marked price & discount: **SP = MP(1 - discount%/100)** — discount is on **MP**, profit on **CP**.

## Handy shortcuts

- **Successive discounts** a%, b% => single equivalent **a + b - ab/100** (multiply (1-a/100)(1-b/100)).
- **Dishonest dealer** selling at CP with a false weight: **gain% = error/(true value - error) x 100** (900 g 'kg' => 100/900 = 11.11%).
- **Successive selling** through sellers: final price = CP x (1+p1/100)(1+p2/100)...
- **CP = 100 method:** set cost price to 100 to turn mark-up + discount into one clean SP.

**Worked example:** Marked 50% above cost, 20% discount. CP=100 => MP=150 => SP = 150 x 0.8 = 120 => **profit 20%**.

**Common trap:** subtracting the discount% from the mark-up% (50 - 20 = 30%) — wrong, because they act on different bases.
keyPoints: Profit%/Loss% are computed on Cost Price; SP = CP(1 +/- pct/100).
SP = MP(1 - discount%/100): discount on MP, profit on CP.
Successive discounts a%, b% = single a + b - ab/100.
Dishonest dealer at CP with false weight: gain% = error/(true - error) x 100.
Successive selling: final = CP x (1+p1/100)(1+p2/100)...
CP=100 shortcut converts any mark-up + discount into a direct profit%.
items.mnemonic: Discount is on MP, profit is on CP — never mix the bases.
items.source: local APPSC Group-1 Quantitative Reasoning PDFs — Discount & MP.txt, Successive discount.txt, Successive Selling.txt

items.title: Partnership & Mixtures/Alligation
items.body:
## Partnership (profit sharing)

- Each partner's share of profit is **proportional to Capital × Time invested**.
- Equal time ⇒ share ratio = **capital ratio**. Different times ⇒ use **capital-months** (capital × months).
- Steps: form the ratio C₁T₁ : C₂T₂ : …, add the parts, take each partner's fraction of the profit.

**Worked example.** A ₹5,000 for 12 mo, B ₹6,000 for 6 mo → 60,000 : 36,000 = 5 : 3. On ₹9,600, B = 3/8 × 9,600 = **₹3,600**.

## Mixtures & Alligation

- To blend two ingredients of cost c (cheaper) and d (dearer) to a **mean price m**:

$$\frac{\text{quantity of cheaper}}{\text{quantity of dearer}} = \frac{d - m}{m - c}$$

- The mean price sits **closer** to the ingredient present in greater quantity.

**Worked example.** ₹30/kg and ₹40/kg blended to ₹36/kg → (40−36):(36−30) = 4:6 = **2:3** (cheaper : dearer).

**Trap:** alligation gives the **quantity ratio**, not a price; and the cross-differences go 'dearer−mean over mean−cheaper'.
keyPoints: Partnership share ∝ Capital × Time; equal time ⇒ just the capital ratio.
Different periods: use capital-months (capital × months) before forming the ratio.
Alligation: (dearer − mean):(mean − cheaper) = qty cheaper : qty dearer.
The mean price lies nearer the ingredient used in greater quantity.
Alligation yields a quantity ratio, not a price.
items.mnemonic: Partnership = money × months; Alligation = cross the differences.
items.source: standard APPSC/SSC arithmetic — Partnership; Mixtures & Alligation
